addressed_problems.content: Although robust tickets achieve comparable or better adversarial robustness on several tasks, on SST-2 and IMDB they exhibit a drop in clean accuracy relative to the fine-tuned full model, suggesting a persistent accuracy–robustness trade-off. The precise nature of this trade-off—whether it is inherent to the subnetwork structure or can be mitigated through different mask learning objectives or training procedures—remains an open question. Understanding and potentially resolving this trade-off is crucial for deploying robust tickets where both accuracy and robustness are required.

The relationship between sparsity level and adversarial robustness of robust tickets is non-monotonic: robustness initially improves with increasing sparsity up to a certain threshold, beyond which it deteriorates, eventually collapsing to the level of standard lottery tickets. Moreover, this behavior is task-dependent, as shown by varying sparsity patterns across datasets. A method to predict the optimal sparsity threshold a priori—without exhaustive evaluation—does not yet exist, leaving open the question of how to reliably select sparsity levels that guarantee improved robustness across tasks.

During mask learning, the adversarial loss objective uses a continuous perturbation in the embedding space (via PGD), whereas evaluation is performed using discrete word-substitution attacks (e.g., TextFooler, BERT-Attack). The authors note that this mismatch contributes to the non-smooth robustness performance curve as sparsity varies, indicating that the training-time adversarial objective does not fully capture the behavior under practical attack algorithms. An open problem is how to design a mask learning objective that better aligns with the wide variety of discrete textual attacks, potentially improving the predictability and transferability of robustness.

Experiments demonstrate that the pre-trained initialization of robust tickets is critical for preserving robustness: re-initializing the weights randomly causes a catastrophic drop in robustness, while retaining initialization but removing the subnetwork structure still yields some robustness improvement with longer training. However, the underlying mechanism by which pre-trained weights influence robustness remains poorly understood. Specifically, it is unclear why certain pre-trained weights contribute positively to robustness while others may harm it, and how this relates to the linguistic knowledge encoded in different layers. Further investigation into the causal role of pre-trained initializations in robustness is needed.

The proposed robust ticket extraction method is demonstrated only on BERT-base and evaluated against a limited set of adversarial attacks (TextFooler, BERT-Attack, TextBugger). Whether similar robust subnetworks exist in other PLM architectures (e.g., RoBERTa, T5) or under different pre-training paradigms (e.g., ELECTRA, ALBERT) remains unexplored. Furthermore, the robustness of these tickets against more diverse or stronger threat models (e.g., character-level attacks, substitution-free attacks) has not been tested. Establishing the generality of the Robust Lottery Ticket Hypothesis across architectures, pre-training objectives, and adversarial threat models is an open direction for future work.

Pre-trained language models (PLMs) such as BERT are over-parameterized and achieve strong downstream performance, but they are vulnerable to textual adversarial examples. Prior model-compression and pruning work (e.g., iterative magnitude pruning, IMP) and prior demonstrations of the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis for PLMs focused on recovering sparse subnetworks that match clean accuracy, yet multiple studies report that those pruned subnetworks are less robust to adversarial attacks than the full PLM. Existing adversarial-defense techniques for PLMs (for example, adversarial training and adversarial data augmentation) improve robustness only partially and do not provide a mechanism to discover small subnetworks that are intrinsically more robust. In addition, magnitude-based pruning and IMP are not designed for robustness preservation: they remove weights by magnitude rather than by contribution to adversarial robustness. From an optimization standpoint, learning a sparse subnetwork topology (binary mask over pre-trained weights) for robustness is a discrete, non-differentiable problem that is not directly solvable by gradient methods, and naive estimators (e.g., straight-through) introduce bias. The combined effect of these limitations is that, prior to this work, there is no practical, principled method to (1) identify small subnetworks inside a pre-trained language model whose fine-tuned instances attain substantially improved adversarial robustness while retaining comparable clean accuracy, and (2) perform that identification in a gradient-based framework compatible with adversarial objectives and sparsity control. This gap prevents obtaining memory- and compute-efficient PLM variants that are also more robust, and leaves open why compression often reduces robustness and how to trade off sparsity, accuracy and robustness in PLMs.

nodes.content: In adversarial-robustness research for NLP, practitioners need smaller models that not only preserve clean accuracy but also resist adversarial perturbations, because large PLMs are expensive to deploy and vulnerable to attacks. Prior compressed models or winning tickets were validated mainly on clean accuracy; empirical reports show those subnetworks typically generalize poorly to adversarial test sets and sometimes overfit easy/shortcut samples, so compression has been linked to reduced robustness. Without demonstration that robust subnetworks exist and can be practically extracted, there was no evidence-based path to deploy smaller, robust PLMs or to investigate the structural origins of robustness in PLMs. The conclusion establishes the existence of such robust tickets empirically across multiple datasets, filling that prior gap by providing concrete quantitative benchmarks of clean and adversarial performance for extracted subnetworks.

Researchers lacked a principled, differentiable procedure that (a) directly optimizes a mask topology for adversarial robustness inside a pre-trained language model, and (b) enforces sparsity in a way compatible with gradient-based adversarial objectives. Iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) and straight-through estimators are either not robustness-aware or produce biased gradients for discrete mask variables. Without a soft-relaxation and an explicit adversarial outer objective plus a tractable $L_0$ proxy, there was no practical way to search the combinatorial space of subnetworks guided by adversarial robustness. The proposed mask-learning formulation addresses both the discrete optimization difficulty (via HardConcrete / binary concrete reparameterization) and the robustness objective (via an inner maximization over perturbations and an outer minimization over masks), enabling gradient-based search for robust sparse topologies.

Iterative magnitude pruning requires repeated prune–retrain cycles to reach different sparsity targets and is not tailored to select weights that contribute to adversarial robustness. Practitioners need a practical extraction mechanism that maps learned stochastic mask parameters to a deterministic sparse topology and a retraining recipe that preserves the pre-trained initialization of retained weights. Without such a deterministic extraction rule based on learned confidence (the $\\log\\alpha$ parameters), it would be unclear how to convert the continuous mask optimization result into a deployable fixed subnetwork of a given sparsity level and how to fine-tune it to evaluate the robustness–accuracy tradeoff.

To claim a method reliably discovers robust tickets, one must show that the method's components (sparse mask optimization vs. crude pruning, and inclusion of adversarial training) each contribute to robustness. Prior work did not isolate these components in PLMs for robustness: magnitude-based pruning or random pruning can preserve clean accuracy yet fail under adversarial attacks. Without an ablation that replaces the mask-learning step and removes the adversarial objective, it remains ambiguous which design choices actually produce robustness. The ablation quantifies that both components are necessary to close that gap.

The Lottery Ticket literature posits that initialization and structure are both important for sparse-subnetwork performance, but their relative roles for adversarial robustness in PLMs was unknown. Practitioners need to know whether robustness arises from the sparse topology itself or from retaining specific pre-trained parameter values. Without this knowledge, it is unclear whether one can randomly reinitialize an extracted sparse structure or must preserve pre-trained weights to retain robustness in deployment. The experiments quantify that preserving pre-trained initialization is essential for robust behavior.

Model compression practitioners need guidance on how much sparsity can be applied before robustness degrades. Prior compression work emphasized clean-accuracy preservation and did not characterize robustness as a function of sparsity inside PLMs. Without an empirical characterization, users cannot select sparsity levels that preserve or improve robustness, nor understand whether robustness reliably improves with pruning. The conclusion provides this characterization and signals that robustness selection requires care and may be task-dependent.

For practitioners constrained by compute, demonstrating that a compressed, robustness-improved model also accelerates fine-tuning is important: without such evidence, adopting robust tickets might trade compute for robustness. Prior to this work it was unknown whether robustness-oriented subnetworks could preserve training-speed advantages observed for winning tickets focused on accuracy. The conclusion confirms that robust tickets can also speed up convergence, supporting efficiency claims.

A pre-trained language model, such as BERT-base-uncased, contains subnetworks (termed robust tickets) which, when extracted and fine-tuned in isolation with the preserved pre-trained initialization, achieve substantially higher adversarial robustness while maintaining comparable clean accuracy to the original full model. Concretely, across multiple benchmark datasets (IMDB, AGNEWS, SST-2, QNLI, MNLI, QQP) the extracted robust subnetworks show large improvements in accuracy under adversarial attack (Aua%) relative to the standard fine-tuned BERT-base and to prior robustness methods (FreeLB and InfoBERT): for IMDB the RobustT at 20% sparsity (RobustT_{20%}) subnetwork attains clean accuracy 93.8% and Aua% 55.2 versus the fine-tuned BERT-base clean 94.1% and Aua% 7.8; on AGNEWS RobustT at 40% sparsity (RobustT_{40%}) attains clean 94.9% and Aua% 12.1 versus fine-tuned BERT-base clean 94.7% and Aua% 3.8; on SST-2 RobustT at 30% sparsity (RobustT_{30%}) attains clean 90.9% and Aua% 17.9 versus fine-tuned BERT-base clean 92.0% and Aua% 2.9. These improvements are observed consistently across additional datasets (QNLI, MNLI, QQP).

metadata.narrative: The existence of robust tickets with substantially improved adversarial robustness is well-supported by consistent results across six datasets and three attacks (H1) and by large effect sizes (H2). However, the evaluation is confined to word-substitution attacks with default parameters (P1) and to BERT-base (P3), which limits the generality of the quantitative claims. The baseline fairness concern (P2) is partially mitigated by the large gap over fine-tune but could affect comparisons with FreeLB/InfoBERT. Overall, the conclusion is credible for the tested configuration, but the precise numerical robustness values may not fully transfer to other threat models or architectures.

nodes.title: Robust tickets in BERT-base improve adversarial robustness over standard fine-tuning and prior defense methods

nodes.content:
Robust subnetworks are identified by assigning learnable stochastic binary masks over pre-trained weights and optimizing those masks with an adversarial robust objective plus a smoothing $L_0$ sparsity penalty. Each scalar mask $m_i$ is modeled as a sample from a HardConcrete distribution parameterized by a location parameter $\log \alpha_i$ and temperature $\beta_i$, implemented via the binary concrete (Gumbel-Softmax) reparameterization:
      $$
      \mu_i \sim \mathcal{U}(0,1),
      $$
      $$
      s_i = \sigma\left(\frac{1}{\beta_i}\left(\log\frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i} + \log \alpha_i\right)\right),
      $$
      $$
      m_i = \min\left(1,\;\max\left(0,\; s_i(\zeta - \gamma) + \gamma\right)\right),
      $$
      where $\sigma$ is the sigmoid, $\gamma=-0.1$, $\zeta=1.1$, and $m_i\in[0,1]$ is the relaxed mask used during training. A differentiable proxy for the $L_0$ complexity of the mask vector $m$ is
      $$
      \mathcal{R}(m) = \frac{1}{|m|}\sum_{i=1}^{|m|} \sigma\left(\log\alpha_i - \beta_i \log\frac{-\gamma}{\zeta}\right).
      $$
      Mask optimization is performed by minimizing an adversarial robust objective over masks:
      $$
      \mathcal{L}_{adv}(m) = \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}}\; \max_{\|\delta\|\le \epsilon} \mathcal{L}\big(f(x+\delta; m\odot\theta), y\big),
      $$
      and the combined training objective is
      $$
      \min_{m} \; \mathcal{L}_{adv}(m) + \lambda \mathcal{R}(m),
      $$
      where $f(\cdot; m\odot\theta)$ is the pre-trained language model (PLM) with masked weights, $\theta$ are pre-trained parameters, $\delta$ denotes adversarial perturbations (inner maximization solved by projected gradient descent (PGD)), $\lambda$ is the sparsity regularization strength, and $\odot$ is the elementwise product. This formulation yields a one-shot, differentiable mask-learning procedure that directly searches for subnetworks whose worst-case adversarial loss is small while controlling sparsity via the $L_0$ proxy.

metadata.narrative: The mask-learning method is formally grounded (H3) and empirically binarizes masks (H4), but the threat model mismatch (P5) between continuous Frobenius-norm adversarial training and discrete word-substitution evaluation is a major load-bearing risk acknowledged by the authors. The undocumented temperature hyperparameter (P4) and unvalidated L0 proxy (P6) add secondary uncertainty. The method is a principled approach to learning robust masks, but its practical success for NLP robustness is contingent on the alignment of training and evaluation threat models.

nodes.title: Learnable stochastic binary masks with adversarial objective and L0 sparsity identify robust subnetworks

nodes.content:
After mask optimization, robust subnetworks are extracted in one shot by using the learned mask location parameters $\log\alpha_i$ as confidence scores: at inference the deterministic gate is computed as
      $$
      \hat{m}_i = \min\left(1,\;\max\left(0,\;\sigma(\log\alpha_i)(\zeta - \gamma) + \gamma\right)\right),
      $$
      where $\sigma$ is the sigmoid, $\gamma=-0.1$, $\zeta=1.1$, and weights with the smallest expectations $\alpha_i$ are pruned. The extraction is performed in an unstructured manner across attention-head weights and intermediate MLP neurons of the pre-trained language model (PLM), producing a subnetwork at arbitrary target sparsity in one shot; the extracted robust ticket $f(\hat{m}\odot\theta_0)$ (where $f$ is the PLM and $\theta_0$ denotes the retained pre-trained initializations) is then fine-tuned on the downstream task. This contrasts with iterative magnitude-based pruning and yields flexible sparsity without repeated prune–retrain cycles.

metadata.narrative: The one-shot extraction is straightforward and deterministic (H5), and the mask training with relaxed masks likely accounts for interdependencies during gradient flow, mitigating the interaction concern (P7). The empirical success of downstream fine-tuning (Tables 1,2) confirms that the extraction does not introduce significant degradation. The conclusion is highly credible.

nodes.title: One-shot extraction of robust subnetworks via mask location parameters and fine-tuning with pre-trained initialization

nodes.content: Both the sparse mask learning mechanism and the adversarial loss objective are necessary to obtain the large robustness gains. For IMDB, the full method RobustT at 20% sparsity (RobustT_{20%}) yields accuracy under adversarial attack (Aua%) ≈ 55.6; replacing mask learning with iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) (w/o Mask Learning) yields Aua% ≈ 15.1; removing the adversarial objective (w/o Adv) yields Aua% ≈ 5.4. Similar drops are observed on AGNEWS and SST-2: on AGNEWS RobustT at 40% sparsity (RobustT_{40%}) Aua% 28.5 versus w/o Mask Learning 16.1 and w/o Adv 8.8; on SST-2 RobustT at 30% sparsity (RobustT_{30%}) Aua% 26.7 versus w/o Mask Learning 6.2 and w/o Adv 3.5. These numbers indicate that the adversarial loss objective primarily drives robustness and the mask-learning relaxation (rather than magnitude-based pruning) is essential to discover robustness-relevant connections.

metadata.narrative: The ablation evidence (H6) is compelling and consistent across three datasets, directly demonstrating that both mask learning and adversarial objective are essential relative to the tested alternatives. The only caveat is the limited comparison set (P8), but the magnitude of the drops makes it unlikely that other simple alternatives would match the full method, so the conclusion is strongly supported.

nodes.title: Both sparse mask learning and adversarial objective are necessary for large robustness improvements

nodes.content: The robustness advantage of a robust ticket depends strongly on preserving the original pre-trained weight initializations for the retained connections: when the extracted robust subnetwork is re-initialized randomly (keeping the learned sparse structure but not the original pre-trained values), the adversarial robustness (accuracy under adversarial attack, Aua%) collapses (example: on IMDB, RobustT at 20% sparsity (RobustT_{20%}) Aua% 55.6 with pre-trained initialization; without initialization (w/o Initialization) Aua% 0.2). Conversely, preserving initialization but discarding the learned structure (i.e., keeping full model but re-initializing the removed weights) reduces robustness less dramatically (example: without structure (w/o Structure) Aua% 13.4 on IMDB), and longer training (10 epochs) can partially recover structure-only performance (w/o Structure+Longer Aua% 18.6 on IMDB). Thus, the preserved pre-trained initializations are a primary factor in the observed robustness of extracted tickets.

metadata.narrative: The controlled ablations (H7) convincingly show that initialization is important, but the SST-2 w/o Structure+Longer condition (P9) contradicts the stronger claim that initialization is strictly more important and that structure alone is insufficient. This condition achieves robustness comparable to the robust ticket, indicating that the relative importance depends on dataset and training length. The paper's stated conclusion is too strong; a more nuanced interpretation is necessary.

nodes.title: Pre-trained initialization is the primary factor for robust ticket robustness over structure

nodes.content: As sparsity (compression) increases, adversarial robustness of the discovered robust tickets follows a three-phase trend: (i) initial increase in robustness as unhelpful or harmful weights are removed; (ii) a threshold region where robustness begins to deteriorate while still often remaining above traditional lottery tickets; (iii) at very high compression the robust subnetwork collapses and robustness falls sharply to lottery-ticket levels. This non-monotonic robustness versus sparsity behavior is observed across datasets, and robustness is more sensitive to sparsity than clean accuracy; accuracy typically degrades slowly while robustness shows the three-phase pattern.

metadata.narrative: The thorough sparsity sweep across three datasets (H8) provides consistent evidence for a non-monotonic pattern under TextFooler. However, the lack of error bars (P10) and restriction to a single attack (P11) limit statistical certainty and generality. The three-phase trend is a suggestive empirical observation but not quantitatively robust.

nodes.title: Adversarial robustness of robust tickets shows non-monotonic three-phase pattern with increasing sparsity

nodes.content: The extracted robust subnetworks retain the winning-ticket property of accelerating downstream training: empirically, both clean accuracy and adversarial robustness converge faster during fine-tuning from the robust ticket initialization than when fine-tuning the full BERT or using FreeLB adversarial training, though traditional lottery tickets may converge faster still. Training curves show earlier attainment of high clean accuracy and higher robustness at earlier epochs for robust tickets compared to default fine-tuning and FreeLB.

metadata.narrative: The training curves across three datasets (H9) indicate that robust tickets converge faster than standard fine-tuning and FreeLB, consistent with the winning-ticket property. The single-run presentation (P12) limits statistical confidence, and the acceleration may partly be due to smaller model size, but the consistency across datasets supports the qualitative claim of training acceleration.

nodes.title: Robust tickets accelerate fine-tuning convergence of clean accuracy and adversarial robustness

nodes.content:
In the evaluation of adversarial robustness for BERT-base models fine-tuned on text classification datasets (IMDB, AGNEWS, SST-2) and natural language inference datasets (QNLI, MNLI, QQP), the primary robustness metric accuracy under adversarial attack (Aua%) is defined as the accuracy on adversarial examples generated by three word-substitution attacks (BERT-Attack, TextFooler, TextBugger) using default parameters from the TextAttack library. The test sets are random subsets of the original test splits (500 samples for IMDB, 1000 for the other datasets). These attacks represent a specific class of threat models (word-level substitutions) and the default parameters may not cover worst-case perturbations. The claimed robustness improvements of the robust tickets (e.g., 55.2% vs 7.8% Aua% on IMDB) are therefore contingent on the chosen attack configuration and evaluation protocol.
      Table 1
      Section 4 experimental setup

metadata.failure_mode: If the chosen attacks and parameters do not represent the full adversarial space, the reported Aua% values (e.g., 55.2% on IMDB) may overestimate the true robustness of the subnetwork: a stronger or different attack could reduce Aua% substantially. The conclusion's quantitative claims would then be inflated and the qualitative ranking across methods might change if certain methods are more vulnerable to the missing attacks. The scope of damage would be a narrowing of the valid regime of the conclusion (robustness to the tested attacks, not necessarily to broader threat models).
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper does not justify that the three word-substitution attacks with default parameters are representative of the adversarial space relevant to text classification, nor does it explore other threat models (character-level, sentence-level, larger budgets). The mismatch between the continuous threat model used in training (Frobenius-norm PGD) and the discrete evaluation attacks is acknowledged and suggests that the evaluation attacks may not correspond to the worst-case for the trained mask. Using random subsets reduces evaluation cost but introduces sampling variance that is not quantified.

nodes.title: Limited adversarial attack evaluation scope

nodes.content:
In the comparison of RobustT against baseline defense methods FreeLB and InfoBERT on text classification datasets (IMDB, AGNEWS, SST-2) and additional tasks (QNLI, MNLI, QQP), the hyperparameters for FreeLB and InfoBERT are taken from their original papers (FreeLB implementation from TextAttack, InfoBERT presumably from their code) without explicit per-task tuning. No controlled hyperparameter search for these baselines is reported and it is not confirmed that the same computational budget (e.g., number of epochs, learning rate, batch size) was allocated to all methods. Therefore, the reported performance advantage of RobustT over FreeLB and InfoBERT may be partially or wholly attributable to suboptimal baseline hyperparameters rather than the method itself.
      Table 1

metadata.failure_mode: If FreeLB or InfoBERT can achieve significantly higher Aua% through per-task tuning (e.g., adjusting the number of PGD steps or perturbation budget), the reported superiority of RobustT could be reduced or eliminated. The comparative advantage layer of the conclusion would then be invalid, although the absolute improvement over fine-tune and LTH would remain.
metadata.weakness_reason: It is standard practice to re-tune baselines on each dataset to ensure fair comparison, especially because defense methods often have dataset-specific optimal hyperparameters. The paper's silence on baseline tuning makes it impossible to evaluate whether the gap (e.g., RobustT Aua% 55.2 vs FreeLB 22.6 on IMDB) is due to method quality or hyperparameter mismatch. This is a reproducibility and fairness concern that weakens the comparative claim.

nodes.title: Hyperparameters for baseline methods FreeLB and InfoBERT are not tuned per task, potentially biasing comparisons

nodes.content: All experiments are conducted using the BERT-base-uncased model (12-layer, 768-hidden, 12-heads, approximately 110M parameters). The existence of robust subnetworks with improved adversarial robustness is claimed for pre-trained language models generally, but no experiments on other architectures (e.g., RoBERTa, ALBERT, T5, DistilBERT) are reported. The properties of BERT-base (e.g., its specific pre-training objective, model depth, and width) may differ from other PLMs, so the finding may not generalize beyond this architecture.

metadata.failure_mode: If other PLMs do not contain robust tickets (e.g., because they are already more robust or have different weight distributions), the conclusion would be restricted to BERT-base, significantly narrowing its applicability. The claimed general existence of robust tickets in PLMs would be unsupported for models beyond BERT.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper does not argue that BERT-base is representative of all PLMs; in fact, different PLMs have different pre-training objectives (MLM vs. permuted language modeling, etc.) and different representational properties that could affect the existence and characteristics of robust tickets. Without experiments on other architectures, the claim's generality is untested.

nodes.title: Generalization limited to BERT-base

nodes.content:
In the HardConcrete mask learning procedure, each mask m_i follows a HardConcrete distribution with temperature β_i and location log α_i. The constants γ = -0.1 and ζ = 1.1 are fixed across all experiments. The temperature β_i is not listed in the reported hyperparameters and its value or tuning strategy is not discussed. The quality of the binary concrete relaxation depends critically on β: as β → 0, the relaxation becomes Bernoulli; as β → ∞, the relaxation becomes uniform. The sensitivity of the results to β or to the fixed constants is not evaluated, so the robustness of the method to these choices is unknown.
      Eq.2, Eq.3

metadata.failure_mode: If the chosen (but unreported) temperature yields a poor approximation, the learned masks may be far from binary during training, leading to suboptimal mask extraction at inference. The quantitative robustness results could be improved or degraded with a different temperature, making the method's performance sensitive to this undocumented choice. The method's reliability would be questionable.
metadata.weakness_reason: The binary concrete distribution's effectiveness as a relaxation is well-known to depend on temperature; in practice, β is annealed during training. The paper does not mention any annealing schedule. Without specifying β, the reproducibility of the mask learning is compromised, and the claim that the method is "principled" is partially undermined by undocumented hyperparameters.

nodes.title: Temperature β of HardConcrete distribution is not specified and its sensitivity is unevaluated

nodes.content:
The adversarial loss objective used during mask learning defines perturbations δ constrained by the Frobenius norm on the continuous embedding space, solved by projected gradient descent (PGD) with step size η and a fixed number of steps K. However, the downstream robustness evaluation uses word-substitution attacks (BERT-Attack, TextFooler, TextBugger) that operate on discrete tokens and do not respect the Frobenius norm constraint. This gap is acknowledged: the robustness curve is not smooth in part due to this mismatch. Therefore, the mask optimization minimizes worst-case loss under a continuous threat model, while the evaluation measures performance under a different threat model; the observed robustness improvements on the evaluation attacks may not be optimal for those attacks.
      Eq.6, Eq.7
      Section 5.1

metadata.failure_mode: If the threat model mismatch is severe, the masks learned to minimize continuous perturbations may not be robust to discrete word substitutions; the observed high Aua% under TextFooler et al. could be a serendipitous side effect that does not extend to other discrete attacks or constrained budgets. The method's generalizability to different attack types would be limited, and the conclusion that it finds robust tickets would be contingent on the specific evaluation attacks.
metadata.weakness_reason: The Frobenius-norm constrained PGD attack operates on continuous embeddings, which is a standard proxy in NLP adversarial training, but its alignment with word-level substitution attacks is not formally justified. The paper's own observation of a non-smooth robustness curve suggests that the gap has empirical consequences. Without an analysis of how well the training threat model transfers to the evaluation threat model, the method's claimed robustness may be partly coincidental.

nodes.title: Threat model mismatch: continuous Frobenius-norm constraints during training vs discrete word-substitution attacks during evaluation

nodes.content:
The L0 sparsity penalty used during mask learning is a smoothed approximation: for each mask i, the contribution to the penalty is σ(log α_i - β_i log(-γ/ζ)). The regularization strength λ is chosen per dataset from the range [0.1,1]. It is not verified that this proxy accurately predicts the true L0 count of the extracted binary masks. Any discrepancy between the proxy and the actual number of zero-masks could affect the reported sparsity levels and the sparsity-robustness analysis.
      Eq.4
      Eq.5

metadata.failure_mode: If the proxy overestimates sparsity (i.e., predicts a higher L0 penalty than the actual number of zeroed weights), then the subnetworks reported as 20% sparsity might actually be less sparse, and the observed robustness improvements might occur at different true sparsity levels. The sparsity-robustness patterns (three-phase) could be misaligned with the x-axis labels in Fig.2, potentially altering the interpretation of when robustness peaks or collapses.
metadata.weakness_reason: The L0 proxy is a known approximation from Louizos et al., but its accuracy depends on the distribution of log α_i and the sigmoid function. The paper does not provide a scatter plot or correlation statistics between the proxy and the actual binary mask after thresholding. Without such validation, the reported sparsity levels (e.g., 20%, 40%) may not accurately reflect the fraction of weights pruned, introducing uncertainty in the sparsity-robustness characterization (Conclusion 6).

nodes.title: Smoothed L0 sparsity proxy may not accurately predict true L0 count of extracted binary masks

nodes.content: After training the mask parameters over the full set of pre-trained weights in an unstructured manner, the extraction procedure prunes all weights with the smallest deterministic gate values simultaneously in one shot to reach the target sparsity (e.g., 20%, 40%, 30%). This simultaneous removal disregards potential dependencies between weights: pruning one connection may affect the utility of another, but the mask training with relaxed masks (all weights present during gradient computation) may partially mitigate this. It is not examined whether one-shot joint pruning degrades performance relative to the mask training performance, or whether an iterative extraction (e.g., gradually increasing sparsity) would improve robustness.

metadata.failure_mode: If the interaction effect is large, the one-shot extraction could produce a subnetwork that underperforms relative to the mask training performance (e.g., lower clean accuracy or robustness than expected). The conclusion that the one-shot extraction yields a high-quality subnetwork would be weakened; the practical benefit of one-shot extraction would be reduced if iterative extraction yields better performance.
metadata.weakness_reason: In the lottery ticket literature, iterative magnitude pruning is often used to avoid the interaction problem because the magnitude order can change after each pruning round. The HardConcrete relaxation during training allows all weights to be present, so the mask optimization accounts for interactions at the gradient level, but after extraction, the removed weights are gone; the remaining weights may not function as expected because they were trained in the presence of the now-removed weights. The extent of this issue is not investigated.

nodes.title: One-shot extraction disregards potential weight dependencies; iterative extraction is not examined

nodes.content:
The ablation study compares the full method RobustT against two variants: w/o Mask Learning, which replaces mask learning with iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) while keeping the adversarial objective during fine-tuning, and w/o Adv, which removes the adversarial objective but keeps mask learning. The comparison does not include other robustness-aware pruning methods (e.g., Hydra from Sehwag et al. 2020, which prunes based on importance scores with adversarial training) or other mask-learning variants (e.g., using straight-through Gumbel-Sigmoid with adversarial objective). Therefore, the conclusion that both mask learning and adversarial objective are necessary is established only relative to the specific alternatives tested; it does not preclude the existence of other methods that achieve similar robustness without both components.
      Table 3

metadata.failure_mode: If another method (e.g., IMP with adversarial training during pruning, or a different mask-learning scheme) can achieve comparable Aua% (e.g., >50% on IMDB), then the claim that the specific mask learning mechanism is necessary for large robustness gains would be false. The conclusion would need to be narrowed to "IMP without adversarial training during pruning is insufficient" (which is trivial), rather than "mask learning (as formulated) is necessary."
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper claims necessity of the specific mask learning (HardConcrete) and adversarial objective, but the ablation only tests one alternative for mask learning (IMP) and one alternative for the objective (none). This is a limited comparison. Other methods that incorporate adversarial training into pruning (e.g., Vemparala et al. 2021 for vision) might also produce robust subnetworks without the HardConcrete relaxation. The paper does not engage with this literature.

nodes.title: Ablation study compares only two variants; other robustness-aware pruning methods are not included

nodes.content:
In the analysis of the importance of initialization versus structure, the condition w/o Structure+Longer on SST-2 uses the full BERT model with weights removed according to the robust ticket structure (i.e., masking out the pruned weights, but re-initializing the kept weights and adding back the pruned weights with re-initialization) and is fine-tuned for 10 epochs. It achieves a TextFooler accuracy under adversarial attack (Aua%) of 27.5%, which is higher than RobustT's 26.7% (fine-tuned for 3 epochs). This result shows that on SST-2, the structure alone (without the learned pre-trained initialization) can outperform the robust ticket when given longer training, contradicting the claim that initialization of retained pre-trained weights is critical for robustness and structure alone is insufficient.
      Table 4

metadata.failure_mode: If the conclusion as stated is taken at face value, it would be false for SST-2 (where structure alone with longer training matches or exceeds the robust ticket). The paper's conclusion would be invalid for at least this dataset and training setting. The proper conclusion should be that initialization is important but not strictly necessary on all tasks, and structure can compensate with extended training.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper includes this data point but still asserts the strong conclusion. The result is from the same controlled experiment, so it cannot be dismissed. It indicates that the claim is too strong; the relative importance of initialization and structure depends on the dataset and training duration.

nodes.title: On SST-2, structure with longer training outperforms robust ticket, contradicting initialization-critical claim

nodes.content:
The robustness versus sparsity curves for IMDB, AGNEWS, and SST-2 are presented as single runs without error bars, confidence intervals, or any measure of variance across independent mask learning runs or fine-tuning seeds. The three-phase pattern (robustness improves, then decreases, then collapses) is described qualitatively. Without multiple runs, it is unclear whether this pattern is reproducible or an artifact of a single trial.
      Fig.2

metadata.failure_mode: If the pattern is not reproducible, the characterization of a three-phase trend would be unsupported. The conclusion that robustness non-monotonically varies with sparsity may be inaccurate, and the practical guidance (e.g., optimal sparsity thresholds) would be unreliable.
metadata.weakness_reason: It is standard in ML to report averages over multiple seeds for such analyses, as the mask learning and fine-tuning can have variance. The paper does not provide seed information. The claimed phases may be due to random fluctuations, especially at higher sparsities where the performance can be noisy.

nodes.title: Sparsity analysis lacks error bars and multiple runs

nodes.content:
The robustness versus sparsity analysis evaluates only the TextFooler attack. Other attacks (BERT-Attack, TextBugger) are not included in this analysis. There is a gap between the adversarial training objective and real attacks; the sparsity pattern under alternative attacks may differ from that observed under TextFooler.
      Fig.2 caption

metadata.failure_mode: If under BERT-Attack or TextBugger the sparsity pattern is monotonic or shows a different peak, then the claimed three-phase trend would be attack-specific and not general. The conclusion about the sparsity effect would be limited to TextFooler, reducing its utility.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's main Table 1 shows that the rank ordering of methods can differ across attacks (e.g., on IMDB, InfoBERT Aua% 26.0 under BERT-Attack vs 32.4 under TextFooler). The sparsity effect may similarly vary by attack, but this is not tested.

nodes.title: Sparsity analysis uses only the TextFooler attack

nodes.content:
The training acceleration results show convergence curves of clean accuracy and accuracy under adversarial attack (Aua%) against TextFooler across three datasets (IMDB, SST-2, AGNEWS) for the robust ticket, traditional lottery ticket, FreeLB, and standard fine-tuning. The curves are shown for a single run per condition; no error bars or multiple-seed statistics are provided. Additionally, the computational cost of the mask learning phase is not included, so any reported acceleration applies only to the fine-tuning phase and may not reflect end-to-end speedup.
      Fig.4

metadata.failure_mode: If the convergence advantage is not statistically significant, the claim that robust tickets accelerate training would be unsupported. Additionally, if the mask learning phase is costly (e.g., PGD steps per batch), the total time to obtain a robust ticket might exceed that of standard fine-tuning, undermining the practical acceleration benefit.
metadata.weakness_reason: Single-run curves can be influenced by random seed and training dynamics. Without multiple seeds, the visual impression of faster convergence may not be statistically significant. Moreover, the acceleration could be an artifact of different learning rates or initialization, but the paper does not control for these. The exclusion of mask learning cost means the actual training time including mask learning might be longer than standard fine-tuning.

nodes.title: Training curves shown for single run without error bars or end-to-end cost

nodes.content: Across six datasets—IMDB, AGNEWS, SST-2 (text classification), QNLI, MNLI, QQP (natural language inference/paraphrase)—and under three word-substitution attacks (BERT-Attack, TextFooler, TextBugger), the extracted robust tickets consistently achieve higher Aua% (accuracy under attack) than standard fine-tuned BERT, traditional lottery tickets (LTH), FreeLB, and InfoBERT, while maintaining clean accuracy within 1-2 percentage points (Tables 1 and 2). This consistency across diverse tasks and attacks demonstrates that the robustness improvement is not a single-dataset or single-attack artifact.

metadata.credit: The multi-dataset and multi-attack evaluation guards against the failure that the observed improvement is specific to one dataset or one attack. It underwrites the qualitative direction (robust tickets exist with better robustness) and the quantitative magnitude (the improvement is substantial and consistent). The scope of credit is full underwriting for the existence claim across the tested tasks and attacks, though not beyond the word-substitution threat model.

nodes.title: Multi-dataset multi-attack consistent improvement

nodes.content: On IMDB, RobustT20% achieves a TextFooler Aua% of 55.6%, compared to fine-tuned BERT's 12.2% and the lottery ticket LTH20%'s 7.2%, a 4- to 8-fold relative improvement. Clean accuracy is 93.8% vs 94.1% for fine-tune. Similarly large margins are observed on AGNEWS (RobustT40% Aua% 28.5 vs fine-tune 14.9) and QQP (RobustT30% Aua% 47.2 vs fine-tune 24.8).

metadata.credit: The large effect size guards against the failure that the robustness improvement is small or practically negligible. It underwrites the quantitative magnitude layer: the improvement is substantial enough to be practically relevant, even if the absolute values have small biases. Scope: supports the practical significance of the method.

nodes.title: Large effect size of robustness improvement

nodes.content: The mask learning method models each binary mask as a sample from a HardConcrete distribution with location parameter log α_i and temperature β_i (Eq.2-3), enabling gradient-based optimization via the Gumbel-Softmax reparameterization. This avoids the biased gradient estimates of straight-through estimators and provides a principled way to learn discrete mask topologies with respect to a differentiable loss (Eq.8).

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure that the mask optimization is infeasible due to the discrete, non-differentiable nature of the binary mask. It underwrites the formal validity of the method: the gradient-based search is grounded in a well-established relaxation. Scope: full underwriting of the feasibility of differentiable mask learning.

nodes.title: Principled differentiable relaxation for binary masks

nodes.content: During mask training on SST-2 (Fig.1), over 90% of the learned stochastic masks converge to values very close to 0 or 1 (i.e., mi ≤ 0.01 or mi ≥ 0.99) for various regularization strengths λ, and the L0 proxy R(m) converges to a stable value. This indicates that the HardConcrete relaxation successfully binarizes the masks, so that the subsequent deterministic extraction via Eq.5 is well justified.

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure that the learned masks remain intermediate-valued, preventing clean subnetwork extraction. It underwrites the operationalization of the method: the training procedure effectively binarizes the topology. Scope: regime-bounded to the datasets where Fig.1 is shown (SST-2), but similar behavior is claimed for other datasets in Appendix A.

nodes.title: Empirical binarization of learned masks

nodes.content: After mask training, subnetworks at any target sparsity can be extracted by a single pruning step: for each weight, the deterministic mask value is computed via Eq.5, and weights with the smallest mask values are removed. No iterative prune-retrain cycles are needed, and the procedure yields a subnetwork of arbitrary sparsity in one shot.

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure that extraction requires multiple costly pruning rounds. It underwrites the practicality and efficiency of the method. Scope: supports the one-shot claim as a practical advantage.

nodes.title: One-shot extraction with flexible sparsity

nodes.content: In the ablation study (Table 3), on IMDB, replacing the proposed mask learning with IMP (w/o Mask Learning) reduces TextFooler Aua% from 55.6% to 15.1%, and removing the adversarial objective (w/o Adv) reduces it to 5.4%. On AGNEWS, the drops are from 28.5% to 16.1% and 8.8% respectively. On SST-2, from 26.7% to 6.2% and 3.5%. The standard fine-tuned BERT obtains 5.0% on SST-2. These results are large and consistent across three datasets, powerfully illustrating the necessity of both components.

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure that the robustness improvement could be attributed to either component alone. It underwrites the causal attribution that both mask learning and adversarial objective are essential. The controlled removal shows directly that neither IMP with adversarial training nor mask learning without adversarial objective achieves comparable robustness. Scope: full underwriting of the necessity of both components under the tested conditions and comparisons.

nodes.title: Dramatic and consistent ablation results

nodes.content: The controlled ablation (Table 4) isolates initialization and structure: using random reinitialization of the robust ticket weights (w/o Initialization) collapses Aua% to near zero across datasets (0.2% IMDB, 0.4% AGNEWS, 2.1% SST-2). Discarding the sparse structure but retaining pre-trained initialization (w/o Structure) yields intermediate Aua% (13.4%, 21.8%, 15.7%), and longer training on w/o Structure improves these values (18.6%, 24.6%, 27.5%). This design causally identifies that initialization is a major factor, and structure provides additional benefit.

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure that we attribute robustness entirely to structure without testing initialization. It underwrites the causal understanding that pre-trained initialization is a critical contributor to robustness. Scope: strongly supports the importance of initialization, though the strong conclusion that "structure alone is insufficient" is nuanced by SST-2 w/o Structure+Longer.

nodes.title: Controlled causal experiment for initialization vs structure

nodes.content: For IMDB, AGNEWS, and SST-2, robustness (Aua% under TextFooler) is measured at many sparsity levels from 0% to 90%+ (Fig.2). In all three datasets, a consistent three-phase pattern emerges: as sparsity increases, robustness initially improves, reaches a peak, then deteriorates, and at extreme sparsity collapses to levels comparable to traditional lottery tickets. This thorough sweep provides an empirical characterization of the sparsity-robustness relationship.

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure that the sparsity effect is random or dataset-specific. It underwrites the qualitative trend (non-monotonic) as an empirical property, providing guidance for selecting sparsity levels. Scope: establishes the relationship for the evaluated datasets under TextFooler.

nodes.title: Thorough empirical sparsity sweep across three datasets

nodes.content: Training curves (Fig.4) for IMDB, SST-2, and AGNEWS show that robust tickets (e.g., RobustT20% on IMDB) achieve higher clean accuracy and Aua% (TextFooler) in early epochs compared to standard fine-tuning and FreeLB. The robust tickets converge to their final performance levels roughly 1-2 epochs earlier than fine-tuning, and traditional lottery tickets converge even faster. This acceleration is observed across all three datasets, indicating that robust tickets retain the winning-ticket property of faster training.

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure that robust tickets trade compute for robustness (longer training). It underwrites the claim that robust tickets preserve training speed advantages. Scope: supports the efficiency benefit on the tested datasets, though the single-run nature limits statistical certainty.

nodes.title: Training acceleration demonstrated on three datasets

steps.reasoning: Start from the established empirical finding that both the adversarial mask-learning method (conclusion 2) and the necessity of its components (conclusion 4) have been validated; these upstream results justify evaluating the final claim that PLMs contain robust tickets.

State the evaluation metric and experimental setup: adversarial robustness is reported using the metric Aua% (the adversarial evaluation percentage reported after TextFooler attacks as used in the experiments), and clean accuracy is the standard test-set accuracy; experiments compare fine-tuned BERT (the full model baseline), prior robustness methods (e.g., FreeLB and InfoBERT), traditional lottery tickets (LTH at given sparsity), random pruning baselines, and the proposed RobustT subnetworks at specified sparsities; results are reported in the main result table and task-specific tables.
Table 1

Present the key IMDB comparison from the main results: the fine-tuned BERT baseline attains clean accuracy $94.1\\%$ and Aua% $7.8$ under BERT-Attack (as reported in the table), while the extracted robust subnetwork RobustT$_{20\\%}$ attains clean accuracy $93.8\\%$ and Aua% $55.2$ (RobustT$_{20\\%}$ row). Thus, the robust ticket maintains clean accuracy comparable to the full model (a $0.3$ percentage-point decrease) while producing a large absolute increase in adversarial robustness (Aua% from $7.8$ to $55.2$).
Table 1

Present the AGNEWS comparison: the fine-tuned BERT baseline attains clean accuracy $94.7\\%$ and Aua% $3.8$, whereas RobustT$_{40\\%}$ attains clean accuracy $94.9\\%$ and Aua% $12.1$ (RobustT$_{40\\%}$ row). Thus RobustT$_{40\\%}$ preserves or slightly improves clean accuracy while substantially increasing Aua% from $3.8$ to $12.1$.
Table 1

Present the SST-2 comparison: the fine-tuned BERT baseline attains clean accuracy $92.0\\%$ and Aua% $2.9$, while RobustT$_{30\\%}$ attains clean accuracy $90.9\\%$ and Aua% $17.9$ (RobustT$_{30\\%}$ row). Here RobustT$_{30\\%}$ incurs a modest clean-accuracy decrease (about $1.1$ percentage points) but achieves a large absolute increase in adversarial robustness (Aua% from $2.9$ to $17.9$).
Table 1

Extend to additional GLUE-style tasks: Table 2 reports results on QNLI, MNLI and QQP where RobustT$_{30\\%}$ consistently attains higher Aua% than the fine-tuned BERT baseline (for example QNLI: fine-tune Aua% TextFooler $4.7$, RobustT$_{30\\%}$ Aua% $17.0$; MNLI: fine-tune Aua% $7.7$, RobustT$_{30\\%}$ Aua% $18.4$; QQP: fine-tune Aua% $24.8$, RobustT$_{30\\%}$ Aua% $47.2$), while maintaining comparable clean accuracy levels reported in the table. These task-level improvements corroborate the IMDB/AGNEWS/SST-2 findings and demonstrate consistency across diverse datasets.
Table 2

Synthesize the empirical claim: based on the reported experimental comparisons across multiple benchmark datasets and attacks, conclude that a pre-trained language model contains subnetworks (termed robust tickets) which, when the subnetwork is extracted and fine-tuned in isolation with the preserved pre-trained initialization, achieve substantially higher adversarial robustness (as measured by Aua%) while maintaining comparable clean accuracy to the original full model; the numerical examples above (IMDB, AGNEWS, SST-2) and task-level results (QNLI, MNLI, QQP) provide concrete evidence.
Table 1
Table 2

Define the objects of optimization: let $f(\\cdot;\\theta)$ denote a pre-trained language model (PLM) with parameters $\\theta$; let $m$ denote a mask vector with the same dimensionality as $\\theta$ and entries $m_i$ that will zero out or keep individual weights via the Hadamard (elementwise) product $m \\odot \\theta$; during training the goal is to learn $m$ so that the masked model $f(\\cdot; m\\odot\\theta)$ yields a small worst-case adversarial loss while being sparse.

Model each scalar mask $m_i$ as a relaxed stochastic binary variable using the hard concrete distribution: introduce a location parameter $\\log\\alpha_i$ and temperature $\\beta_i$, draw $\\mu_i\\sim\\mathcal{U}(0,1)$ (where $\\mathcal{U}(0,1)$ denotes the uniform distribution on $(0,1)$), compute the intermediate $s_i$ and the relaxed mask $m_i$ by
$$
\\mu_i \\sim \\mathcal{U}(0,1),
$$
$$
s_i = \\sigma\\left(\\frac{1}{\\beta_i}\\left(\\log\\frac{\\mu_i}{1-\\mu_i} + \\log\\alpha_i\\right)\\right),
$$
$$
m_i = \\min\\left(1,\\;\\max\\left(0,\\; s_i(\\zeta - \\gamma) + \\gamma\\right)\\right),
$$
where $\\sigma(\\cdot)$ denotes the sigmoid function, and constants $\\gamma=-0.1$ and $\\zeta=1.1$. These formulas realize a HardConcrete relaxation (a smoothing approximation of Bernoulli) and permit gradient-based optimization via the reparameterization $\\mu_i$ sample; this modeling choice is based on prior work on learning sparse neural networks through $L_0$ regularization. 
Louizos et al. (2018)

Explain the rounding behavior and role of the parameters: the binary-concrete intermediate $s_i$ behaves like a softened Bernoulli with expectation controlled by $\\alpha_i$, and as $\\beta_i\\to 0$ samples from $s_i$ approach Bernoulli samples with probability $\\alpha_i$; the clipping with $\\gamma$ and $\\zeta$ maps $s_i$ into the interval $[0,1]$ and thresholds values sufficiently large or small toward exact 1 or 0 respectively, enabling eventual discrete mask behavior at convergence.

Introduce a differentiable proxy for $L_0$ sparsity: define the sparsity regularizer $\\mathcal{R}(m)$ as the empirical probability that a mask component is nonzero under the hard-concrete distribution,
$$
\\mathcal{R}(m) = \\frac{1}{|m|} \\sum_{i=1}^{|m|} \\sigma\\left(\\log \\alpha_i - \\beta_i \\log\\frac{-\\gamma}{\\zeta}\\right),
$$
where $|m|$ denotes the number of mask entries. This quantity serves as a smooth approximation to the $L_0$ norm (the fraction of retained weights) and is differentiable with respect to $\\log\\alpha_i$ and $\\beta_i$, permitting gradient-based sparsity control.

Define the adversarial robust objective over masks: denote by $(x,y)\\sim\\mathcal{D}$ a data point from the downstream dataset $\\mathcal{D}$, and let $\\delta$ denote input perturbations constrained by $\\|\\delta\\|\\le\\epsilon$ where $\\epsilon$ is an attacker budget. Then define the adversarial loss as the outer minimization over masks of the inner worst-case perturbation loss:
$$
\\mathcal{L}_{adv}(m) = \\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\\sim\\mathcal{D}}\\; \\max_{\\|\\delta\\|\\le \\epsilon} \\mathcal{L}\\big(f(x+\\delta; m\\odot\\theta), y\\big),
$$
where $\\mathcal{L}(\\cdot,\\cdot)$ is the classification loss (e.g., cross-entropy). This objective explicitly searches for masks that minimize the model's loss on adversarially perturbed inputs.

Describe how the inner maximization is solved in practice: use projected gradient descent (PGD) to approximate the inner maximization over $\\delta$, iterating the perturbation update
$$
\\delta_{k+1}=\\prod_{\\|\\delta\\|\\le\\epsilon}\\left(\\delta_k + \\eta \\frac{g(\\delta_k)}{\\|g(\\delta_k)\\|}\\right),
$$
where $g(\\delta_k)=\\nabla_x \\mathcal{L}\\big(f(x+\\delta_k; m\\odot\\theta), y\\big)$, $\\eta$ is a step size, and $\\prod_{\\|\\delta\\|\\le\\epsilon}(\\cdot)$ denotes projection back onto the allowed perturbation ball; the final perturbation $\\delta_K$ is used to form adversarial examples $x+\\delta_K$ for the outer minimization. This follows the standard adversarial training inner-loop approach.
Madry et al. (2018)

Combine sparsity and robustness into a single differentiable training objective over the stochastic masks: introduce a scalar sparsity regularization weight $\\lambda$ and minimize
$$
\\min_m \\; \\mathcal{L}_{adv}(m) + \\lambda \\mathcal{R}(m),
$$
where $\\mathcal{L}_{adv}(m)$ is defined above, $\\mathcal{R}(m)$ is the smooth $L_0$ proxy, and optimization variables are the mask parameters (the location parameters $\\log\\alpha_i$ and possibly temperatures $\\beta_i$). This casts mask discovery as a one-shot, end-to-end differentiable optimization problem that directly targets adversarial robustness while controlling sparsity.

Summarize the practical algorithmic consequences: optimizing the mask parameters via gradient-based methods (with PGD used to approximate the inner maximization) yields a one-shot mask-learning pruning method that (a) directly searches for subnetworks whose worst-case adversarial loss is small and (b) controls sparsity through the $L_0$ proxy $\\mathcal{R}(m)$, avoiding iterative magnitude-based prune–retrain cycles in favor of a single differentiable procedure.
Louizos et al. (2018)

Treat the mask-learning pruning method and the learned mask location parameters $\\log\\alpha_i$ (from the previous conclusion) as established and available; these quantities are the outputs of the differentiable adversarial $L_0$ mask optimization and are treated here as given.

Define the deterministic extraction gate used at inference: compute the deterministic mask estimate $\\hat{m}_i$ from the learned location parameter $\\log\\alpha_i$ via the hard concrete gate formula
$$
\\hat{m}_i = \\min\\left(1,\\;\\max\\left(0,\\;\\sigma(\\log\\alpha_i)(\\zeta - \\gamma) + \\gamma\\right)\\right),
$$
where $\\sigma(\\cdot)$ denotes the sigmoid function and constants $\\gamma$ and $\\zeta$ are as in the mask-learning procedure; this gate maps the learned expectation $\\sigma(\\log\\alpha_i)$ into a 0–1 deterministic value for pruning.

Use the learned expectations $\\alpha_i$ (equivalently $\\log\\alpha_i$) as confidence scores to rank and prune weights: treat $\\alpha_i$ as the expectation (confidence) of retaining the $i$-th connection under the learned hard-concrete distribution, and prune (set to zero) the parameters whose corresponding $\\alpha_i$ are smallest so as to reach a target sparsity; this yields an unstructured pruning mask $\\hat{m}$.

Clarify the retained initialization used for retraining: denote by $\\theta_0$ the original pre-trained parameter values (the pre-trained initialization) corresponding to the full model before any task fine-tuning; construct the extracted robust ticket as the masked model $f(\\hat{m}\\odot\\theta_0)$, i.e., the subnetwork that preserves the pre-trained values of the retained connections and zeros out pruned weights.

Describe the retraining (fine-tuning) procedure for the extracted ticket: fine-tune the extracted robust ticket $f(\\hat{m}\\odot\\theta_0)$ on the downstream task dataset using the same fine-tuning protocol used for full-model fine-tuning (optimizer, learning rate, epochs, etc.), thereby adapting the retained pre-trained parameters to the task while maintaining the learned sparse structure.

Contrast this one-shot unstructured extraction with iterative magnitude-based pruning: unlike Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) which repeatedly prunes lowest-magnitude weights and re-trains in multiple cycles to reach a target sparsity, the proposed method uses the learned $\\log\\alpha$ in a single extraction step to obtain a subnetwork at any desired sparsity without repeated prune–retrain cycles, and pruning is performed unstructuredly across attention-head weights and intermediate MLP neurons, giving flexible sparsity patterns.

Treat the mask-learning method (conclusion 2) and the one-shot extraction (conclusion 3) as established mechanisms used to produce the models compared in the ablation; these are the upstream results from which the ablation is derived.

Describe the ablation interventions: (a) "w/o Mask Learning" replaces the proposed mask-learning procedure by Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) while keeping other components unchanged, thereby testing whether the mask-learning relaxation is essential; (b) "w/o Adv" removes the adversarial loss objective from the mask-learning optimization and hence tests whether the adversarial outer minimax objective is necessary to discover robustness-relevant connections.

Present the quantitative ablation results from the reported table (TextFooler Aua%): on IMDB the full method (RobustT$_{20\\%}$) yields Aua% $\\approx 55.6$, replacing mask learning with IMP yields Aua% $\\approx 15.1$ (w/o Mask Learning), and removing the adversarial objective yields Aua% $\\approx 5.4$ (w/o Adv); on AGNEWS RobustT$_{40\\%}$ yields Aua% $28.5$ versus w/o Mask Learning $16.1$ and w/o Adv $8.8$; on SST-2 RobustT$_{30\\%}$ yields Aua% $26.7$ versus w/o Mask Learning $6.2$ and w/o Adv $3.5$. These numbers come from the ablation table that reports Aua% after TextFooler attack.
Table 3

Interpret the ablation pattern: observe that removing the adversarial objective ("w/o Adv") typically collapses robustness to low levels, indicating the adversarial outer minimax loss is the primary driver of robustness; replacing mask learning with magnitude-based IMP also substantially degrades robustness (though not as extremely as removing the adversarial objective), indicating that the mask-learning relaxation (the hard-concrete stochastic-mask optimization) is essential for discovering connections relevant to adversarial robustness rather than relying on magnitude alone.

State the operational conclusion: both components — the sparse mask-learning mechanism and the adversarial loss objective — are necessary to obtain the large robustness gains reported for robust tickets; ablations removing either component produce substantially lower Aua% across datasets, supporting the claim that both are required.

Treat the mask-learning method (conclusion 2) as established and the one-shot extraction and fine-tuning procedure (conclusion 3) as available experimental operations; these are the mechanisms used to produce the empirical ablations that follow.

Describe the experimental manipulation "w/o Initialization": after extracting a robust subnetwork $f(\\hat{m}\\odot\\theta_0)$ with learned structure $\\hat{m}$ and retained pre-trained parameters $\\theta_0$, re-initialize the retained parameters randomly (i.e., replace the preserved pre-trained values by random initial values) while keeping the learned sparse structure $\\hat{m}$ unchanged; then fine-tune this re-initialized structured network and evaluate adversarial robustness using the Aua% metric obtained after TextFooler attacks as reported.

Report the empirical results showing collapse of robustness under random re-initialization: for IMDB the original extracted robust ticket (RobustT$_{20\\%}$) attains Aua% $55.6$ when retaining pre-trained initializations, whereas the same sparse structure with random re-initialization ("w/o Initialization") attains Aua% $0.2$; for AGNEWS RobustT$_{40\\%}$ Aua% $28.5$ with pre-trained initialization versus Aua% $0.4$ w/o Initialization; for SST-2 RobustT$_{30\\%}$ Aua% $26.7$ with pre-trained initialization versus Aua% $2.1$ w/o Initialization. These numbers are taken from the reported table of initialization/structure ablations.
Table 4

Describe the complementary experimental manipulation "w/o Structure": preserve the pre-trained initialization for the connections that are retained by the robust ticket, but discard the learned sparse structure by using the full BERT model and re-initializing those weights that the robust ticket had pruned (i.e., keep initializations but not the learned sparsity). Then fine-tune and evaluate adversarial robustness; this isolates the effect of structure versus initialization.

Report "w/o Structure" empirical results that show less catastrophic degradation than "w/o Initialization": for IMDB "w/o Structure" yields Aua% $13.4$ compared to $55.6$ for the full robust ticket, and longer training ("w/o Structure+Longer") recovers some robustness to Aua% $18.6$; similar patterns appear for AGNEWS and SST-2 where "w/o Structure" Aua% values remain substantially above the random re-initialization case but below the full robust-ticket case. These values are from the same ablation table and indicate initialization plays the dominant role.
Table 4

Synthesize the empirical implication: because randomizing the retained pre-trained initializations destroys adversarial robustness almost completely, whereas preserving initializations while discarding structure reduces robustness but to a lesser extent (and can be partially recovered by longer training), conclude that the preserved pre-trained initializations of the retained connections are a primary factor driving the observed robustness of the extracted robust tickets, and that structure alone is insufficient to explain the robustness advantage.

Treat the mask-learning method (conclusion 2) and the extraction protocol (conclusion 3) as established; these provide the mechanisms for producing subnetworks at varying sparsity levels which are evaluated below.

Describe the empirical evaluation across sparsity: the authors vary compression (sparsity) of the discovered robust tickets and evaluate both clean accuracy (the standard test-set accuracy) and adversarial robustness measured by Aua% (the adversarial-attack success/resistance metric obtained after TextFooler attack, as reported in the experiments). The evaluation compares robust tickets to traditional lottery tickets across a range of sparsities.

Report the observed three-phase trend in robustness as sparsity increases (derived from the plotted curves and textual description): (i) an initial phase where robustness increases as sparsity grows because removal of unhelpful or harmful weights helps; (ii) a threshold region where robustness begins to deteriorate though it often remains above the robustness of traditional lottery tickets; (iii) at very high compression the robust subnetwork "collapses" and robustness falls sharply down to levels comparable to lottery tickets. This three-phase description is explicitly stated and illustrated in the robustness-versus-sparsity figure.
Fig.2

State the relative sensitivity of robustness versus clean accuracy: across datasets the clean accuracy typically degrades slowly as sparsity increases, while robustness follows the non-monotonic three-phase pattern and is therefore more sensitive to the pruning level and structure; this observation is supported by the plotted curves where accuracy declines gradually but robustness exhibits the three-phase pattern and sharper drops at high compression.
Fig.2

Note the authors' qualification about curve smoothness: the robustness-performance curve is not as smooth as accuracy, which the authors attribute to a gap between the adversarial mask-learning objective used during training and the real textual attacks used in evaluation; this remark is part of the authors' discussion of observed behavior and possible reasons.

Assume the mask-learning extraction procedure (conclusions 2 and 3) has been used to produce robust tickets and that standard fine-tuning and FreeLB adversarial training baselines have been run under comparable training hyperparameters; these are the experimental setups used to produce training curves.

Describe the training-curve evidence: the authors plot fine-tuning trajectories showing clean accuracy and adversarial accuracy under attack as training proceeds for robust tickets, traditional lottery tickets, default full-model fine-tuning, and FreeLB adversarial training; these plots indicate the relative speed at which each method attains high accuracy and robustness.

Report the empirical conclusion on convergence speed: the training curves demonstrate that both clean accuracy and adversarial robustness converge faster when fine-tuning from the robust ticket initialization than when fine-tuning the full BERT or when using FreeLB adversarial training; specifically, robust tickets attain earlier high clean accuracy and higher robustness at earlier epochs compared to default fine-tuning and FreeLB, while traditional lottery tickets may still converge faster than the robust tickets in some cases.
Fig.4

Summarize the practical implication: because fine-tuning from the extracted robust-ticket initialization accelerates attainment of both accuracy and robustness relative to common baselines, robust tickets retain the "winning-ticket" property of training acceleration (though robustness-oriented constraints make them sometimes slower than purely accuracy-focused lottery tickets), making them useful for faster robust model adaptation.

open_questions.content: The authors acknowledge multiple unresolved scientific issues and limitations that remain after their contributions: (1) The accuracy–robustness trade-off persists for some tasks and sparsity regimes: robust tickets sometimes sacrifice clean accuracy (notably on SST-2 and IMDB) and the precise nature of this trade-off and whether it can be mitigated systematically remains open. (2) The robustness vs. sparsity relationship is task-dependent and non-monotonic; selecting a safe sparsity threshold that preserves or improves robustness is not yet predictable a priori. (3) There is a gap between the adversarial loss objective used during mask learning and the behavior under real textual attack algorithms; the robustness performance curve is not smooth and the authors ascribe part of this to that optimization–evaluation mismatch, leaving open how to align training objectives with diverse practical attacks. (4) The mechanism by which pre-trained initializations influence robustness is not fully understood: while experiments show initialization is critical for preserving robustness in extracted tickets, why certain pre-trained weights harm or help robustness requires further study. (5) The generality of the proposed approach across different PLM architectures, differing pre-training regimes, and a broader set of adversarial threat models beyond the evaluated attacks remains to be explored. These limitations are explicitly noted as directions for future investigation.
